extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders in EPA CAA section 111 rulemakings (state regulators, industry, environmental lawyers, technical commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance and legal standards the EPA uses to identify the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and set emission guidelines for existing electric utility generating units under CAA section 111(d). Covers legal precedent, representativeness, cost considerations, state/EPA roles, technology demonstration, and technical definitions used in analysis and modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolating from testing results to identify an appropriate system
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may extrapolate from testing results, rather than relying on consistent long-term performance, to identify an appropriate system and standard based on that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in Sierra Club v. Costle, EPA analyzed scrubber performance by considering performance during short-term testing periods; short-term test data can be used to inform identification of a system and promulgation of standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of projection/lead time for developing/identifying technology
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may determine a system of emission reduction to be adequately demonstrated based on some amount of projection, even if some aspects of the system are still in development; lead time accommodates development of projected technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes EPA is not relying on this point for purposes of these rules but acknowledges that authorization for lead time is appropriate to accommodate technology development and projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness limits (not exorbitant/industry-survivable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs considered in setting standards may not be 'exorbitant' and may not be 'greater than the industry could bear and survive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case law (Lignite Energy Council; Portland Cement Ass'n v. EPA) and legislative history support these formulations; courts have upheld EPA judgments when costs were high but not unreasonable. Legislative reports treat costs of control as a normal expense of doing business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator's discretion in weighing statutory factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress did not assign specific weight to statutory elements (cost, energy, non-air quality health and environmental impacts), the Administrator is free to exercise discretion in how to weigh those factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's final balancing must be consistent with reasoned agency decisionmaking; case law (New York v. Reilly; NRDC v. EPA) supports deference to EPA's emphasis or deemphasis of particular factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-GHG air pollutants and non-air quality impacts alongside GHG impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing BSER and related measures, EPA may consider the effects of controls on non-GHG air pollutants and non-air quality health and environmental impacts together with effects on GHGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble (citing prior rulemakings) discusses effects of controls on criteria pollutants and other health/environmental impacts in the same analytical context as GHG controls, for convenience and comprehensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER can look toward reasonably projected future developments
rubrics_metrics.description: The best system of emission reduction must 'look toward what may fairly be projected for the regulated future, rather than the state of the art at present.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portland Cement Ass'n v. Ruckelshaus supports consideration of what can be fairly projected for the regulated future when identifying BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological innovation is a factor in statutory balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of technological innovation is encompassed within the statutory factors (cost, energy, non-air quality health and environmental impacts) that EPA must weigh for section 111 standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sierra Club v. Costle holds that mandated balancing 'embraces consideration of technological innovation as part of that balance.' Legislative reports also encourage standards to stimulate development of new technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize from a sample of one if representative
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be sufficient to 'generalize from a sample of one when one is the only available sample, or when that one is shown to be representative of the regulated industry along relevant parameters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider in representativeness include 'feedstock, operation, size and age' of the source. Case law (Nat'l Lime Ass'n v. EPA) supports generalizing from limited samples if adequately representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated facility definition and applicability (40 CFR 60.21a(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'designated facility' means 'any existing facility . . . which emits a designated pollutant and which would be subject to a standard of performance for that pollutant if the existing facility were an affected facility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text (40 CFR 60.21a(b)) defines the term and informs which existing facilities may be subject to a standard when EPA establishes standards for new sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: New vs existing source determination based on proposal date
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111, whether a source is a new source or an existing source (and thus potentially a designated facility) is based on the date that EPA proposes to establish standards of performance for new sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule determines applicability and classification for purposes of section 111 rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA retains primary regulatory role; States implement plans (West Virginia v. EPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although States set the actual rules governing existing power plants under section 111(d), EPA retains the primary regulatory role: EPA determines the amount of pollution reduction and the BSER 'adequately demonstrated' for the source category; States then submit plans with emissions restrictions needed to meet EPA's permissible level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites West Virginia v. EPA and implementing regulations (40 CFR 60.22(b)(5), §§60.23, 60.24) describing EPA's and States' respective roles and plan submission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: State ability to apply less stringent standard for particular units
rubrics_metrics.description: A State may apply a less stringent standard of performance to a particular affected EGU if it demonstrates a fundamental difference between the costs EPA considered and the costs to that unit that makes the degree of limitation (e.g., 40% co-firing) unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with requirements for calculating a less stringent standard at 40 CFR 60.24a(f), States should consider whether it is reasonable for units that cannot cost-reasonably co-fire at 40% to co-fire at lower levels; coal-fired EGUs that can reasonably co-fire any amount of natural gas remain subject to the guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of remaining useful life (RULOF) in unit-specific determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: States may consider the remaining useful life of particular sources when applying standards of performance to affected sources; RULOF applies only when a state is applying a standard of performance to an affected source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's applicability exemptions do not conflict with states' ability to consider RULOF; EPA is responsible for determining category-wide regulation under an emission guideline, while RULOF addresses specific source conditions in state plan application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Rate Improvement (HRI) appropriateness and the rebound effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat rate improvement measures are not appropriate for sources retiring before January 1, 2032 because HRI applied to coal-fired sources achieve few emission reductions and can lead to a 'rebound effect' where CO2 emissions from the source increase rather than decrease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA describes the rebound effect and explains why HRI is not suitable for near-term retiring units (see section VI.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital cost amortization assumptions for cost analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA typically assumes that capital costs can be amortized over 15 years; for CCS, EPA generally assumed a 12-year amortization period because the IRC section 45Q tax credit is available for the first 12 years of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These amortization assumptions are used in determining CCS costs in the regulatory impact analysis and cost calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on relying on EPAct05-assisted projects
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not rely solely on the experience of facilities that received EPAct05 assistance to determine whether a technology is adequately demonstrated, but EPA may rely on such facilities in conjunction with other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA incorporates prior legal interpretation from the 2015 NSPS addressing EPAct05 provisions and how such-assisted projects may be considered in adequacy demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating availability definition for CO2 capture equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating availability is the percent of time that the CO2 capture equipment is available relative to its planned operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric is used to characterize capture-system performance and availability in analyses and project descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical definitions: turndown, duty cycle, train
rubrics_metrics.description: Turndown: ability of a facility to turn down some process value (expressed as a ratio relative to maximum capability); Duty cycle: ratio of gross electricity generated relative to potential generation at nameplate capacity (indicates amount of cycling/load following); Train: a series of connected sequential process equipment (for carbon capture, e.g., quencher, absorber, stripper, compressor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions clarify how EPA discusses operational characteristics, representativeness, and design choices for EGUs and capture systems; they affect analyses of feasibility and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling and timeline assumptions for CO2 transport and pipeline buildout
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative timelines and assumptions used in EPA modeling include an 18-month construction period for a CO2 pipeline in the representative timeline, permitting estimated at 1.5 years, and recognition that actual projects will be spread over longer periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes that some pipeline construction could begin earlier due to ongoing projects; these assumptions inform transport and storage feasibility, cost, and scheduling in the docketed analyses.
